screens.title: Basic Linux Commands and Filesystem Navigation
screens.narratorSegment: Welcome. In this lesson you will learn how Linux arranges files under a single root and how to use the basic commands that let you move around, examine, and manage files. Understanding the Filesystem Hierarchy Standard gives you a reliable mental map so you can predict where configuration files, binaries, logs, and user data live. You will practice confirming your current location, listing directory contents, changing directories with absolute and relative paths, and performing safe file operations like creating, copying, and moving items. We will also cover how to view file content and where to find help using manual pages and quick help flags. A strong grasp of these basics prevents common mistakes, like accidentally deleting important data. For example, the careful use of listing and confirming paths before running a removal command can save hours of recovery work. By the end, you'll be able to navigate confidently and follow a consistent workflow for routine maintenance and troubleshooting.

Module 2 › Chapter 1.3 › Overview
Basic Linux Commands and Filesystem Navigation
Understand the FHS and master the commands that let you navigate and manage files safely on any Linux system.
Orientation

You'll start from the idea that every file and directory has a predictable place. That predictability makes commands portable across distributions. We'll balance command syntax with practical safety checks so you learn both how and why to take each step.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: By the end of this chapter you'll be able to explain how the Linux Filesystem Hierarchy Standard organizes the system, and you'll use basic commands to move around and manage files. Specifically, you'll interpret directory roles such as where system binaries, configuration files, and user data live. You will use the print-working-directory command to confirm your location, the list command to inspect directory contents with useful options, and the change-directory command with absolute and relative paths. You'll also create, copy, move, and remove files and directories while applying safety checks to avoid data loss. Finally, you'll read manual pages and use quick help flags to discover command options independently. These skills are foundational: they let you perform routine administration, troubleshoot file locations, and learn new commands by exploring their documentation. Practically, that means you can navigate to a configuration file, examine it, make a backup copy, and restore it if needed — all without relying on a graphical interface.

screens.title: Filesystem Hierarchy Standard (FHS)
screens.narratorSegment: The Filesystem Hierarchy Standard is the convention that gives every file and directory a predictable place on Linux systems. Rather than drive letters, Linux uses a single root, represented by a forward slash, and organizes everything below it. This consistency matters: if you need to edit system configuration on one distribution, your knowledge about where /etc or /var typically lives transfers to other distributions. For example, system-wide configuration files are kept in /etc while user home directories are under /home. Bin and sbin directories contain executable programs, with /bin holding essential user commands and /sbin containing administrative utilities. The habit of knowing where to look speeds troubleshooting and script writing. A common misconception is that distributions freely rearrange these directories — they do not; the FHS promotes compatibility. In practice, when you search for a log file, you’ll often check /var/log first. Knowing the FHS reduces guesswork and helps you write commands that are robust across systems. Reflect: when you need a configuration file, which top-level directories will you check first and why? Filesystem Hierarchy Standard (FHS) means a single root filesystem with standard top-level directories lets you predict where system and user files live across distributions.. In practical terms, what the fhs is and why a single root matters. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 1.3 › Filesystem Hierarchy
What is the FHS?
A standardized directory layout so files and programs live in predictable locations.
Root (/)
Top of the tree; all paths start here.
/etc
System-wide configuration files and settings.
/home
User personal directories and data.
/var
Variable data such as logs and transient files.
Key Takeaway

Memorize the purpose of a few top-level directories and use them as your first lookup locations when troubleshooting.

Quick reference map
/bin - essential user commands
/sbin - system administration binaries
/usr - user utilities and applications
/opt - optional application packages
/tmp - temporary files
/var - logs and variable data
Misconception check: directories are not arbitrary. They reflect purpose. Look in /etc for configs, /var for logs, and /home for user content.

screens.title: System vs. User Directories
screens.narratorSegment: Linux separates the system-provided executables and libraries from user-installed programs and personal data. Directories like /bin and /sbin store essential binaries used during boot and repair; /lib and /lib64 contain shared libraries required by those programs. In contrast, /usr holds the wider set of utilities and applications, often in /usr/bin and /usr/local. Optional third-party packages sometimes live under /opt. Virtual, runtime, and kernel interfaces appear in /proc and /sys; these are not regular files but views into kernel and process state. A useful mental model is: if you need to run a system maintenance utility as an administrator, check /sbin or /usr/sbin; if you are looking for a user-level program, check /usr/bin or /usr/local/bin. A common error is editing files under /usr directly for package-installed software — prefer /usr/local or /opt for local additions. When you need to inspect libraries, look into /lib or /lib64. Understanding the distinction avoids collisions between packaged files and locally administered resources. System vs. User Directories means system executables and libraries live in protected directories; user utilities and optional software use /usr and /opt, keeping system files stable.. In practical terms, where executables, libraries, and virtual filesystems belong. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 1.3 › System vs User
Protected system directories
Files managed by the OS and packages.
/bin
User-facing essential binaries like listing and copying tools.
/sbin
System administration binaries, often for root use.
/lib, /lib64
Shared libraries required by executables.
User and optional software
Where locally installed or optional apps live.
/usr - user utilities and applications
/usr/local - locally compiled or installed software
/opt - third-party packages and add-ons
Example: If you compile a tool yourself, install it under /usr/local or /opt so package upgrades in /usr don't overwrite your files.

screens.title: Other Important Directories
screens.narratorSegment: Beyond executables and libraries, several directories have distinct runtime or administrative roles. /etc stores system configuration files such as network or service settings; a careful edit here changes system behavior. /home holds personal user data — each account typically has its directory under /home. The root user's personal directory is /root. /var contains variable data like system logs and mail queues; monitor /var/log for troubleshooting. /tmp is for temporary files and usually gets cleared at reboot. Mount points such as /media and /mnt are used for removable devices or temporarily mounted filesystems. Virtual filesystems /proc and /sys present kernel and process information as readable files; for example, /proc exposes process IDs and kernel parameters. A frequent mistake is treating /proc or /sys as normal persistent storage — changes there affect kernel state or are ephemeral. When you need to mount a USB drive, look under /media or /mnt; when diagnosing services, check /etc for configs and /var/log for logs. Other Important Directories means /etc contains configs, /var contains logs, /tmp is ephemeral, and /proc and /sys expose kernel and process state as virtual filesystems.. In practical terms, /etc, /home, /var, /tmp, /media, /mnt, /proc, /sys. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 1.3 › Important Directories
Configuration and user areas
/etc
System configuration files. Editing here changes global behavior.
/home & /root
User home directories and the root user home respectively.
/media, /mnt
Mount points for removable or temporary mounts.
Logs, temp, and kernel interfaces
/var
Variable data such as logs in /var/log.
/tmp
Temporary files; not reliable for long-term storage.
/proc & /sys
Virtual filesystems exposing kernel and process info — not ordinary files.
Scenario: when a service fails, check /etc for its config and /var/log for messages before changing code or restarting the service.

screens.title: Confirming Where You Are: pwd and Home Directory
screens.narratorSegment: When you open a terminal you are placed in your home directory; this is your safe workspace. To confirm your exact location use the print-working-directory command which prints an absolute path from the root. Practically, this prevents running commands in the wrong place. For example, if print-working-directory outputs /home/cohortiauser, you know you are in your personal area and not in /etc or /var. The tilde symbol is a convenient shorthand for the home directory, so using change-directory tilde returns you to your home quickly. Another useful convenience is the dash argument which sends you back to the previous directory, useful when switching between two folders. A common mistake is assuming a graphical prompt aligns with the shell location; always confirm with print-working-directory. Below is a short code example you can type and try in a lab: watch how the path changes and use the dash shortcut to toggle. The habit of printing your working directory before destructive commands is a simple safety practice that pays off. Confirming Where You Are: pwd and Home Directory means use the print-working-directory command and the tilde and dash shortcuts to know and return to safe locations before running commands.. In practical terms, how to confirm your current working directory and use the home shortcut. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 1.3 › pwd & Home
Confirm your location
Use the print-working-directory command to see the absolute path from root.
pwd
# Expected output: /home/cohortiauser

cd /etc
pwd
# Expected output: /etc

cd ~
pwd
# Expected output: /home/cohortiauser

cd -
# Returns to previous directory
Tip: use tilde to jump home and dash to toggle between two directories while working on configs and test files.
Example scenario
You need to edit a config in /etc and test a script in your home directory. Use print-working-directory to confirm where you are before saving changes and toggling back with dash to run tests.
Key Takeaway

Always confirm the absolute path before performing actions that change files or directories.

screens.title: Listing Files with ls
screens.narratorSegment: Listing the contents of a directory is one of the most frequent tasks. The list command in its basic form shows filenames, but combining options gives useful detail. For example, list with long format shows permissions, ownership, size, and modification time, which is essential when troubleshooting permission problems or identifying large files. Adding human-readable sizes converts byte counts into kilo, mega, or giga units so you can scan sizes quickly. The option to show hidden files reveals items starting with a dot, which include shell configuration files. Combining these options is common: long, all, and human-readable together give a compact and informative view. A misconception is relying on graphical file managers for hidden items; hidden files exist and matter at the shell. Below is a short walkthrough you can run to see these outputs. Practice interpreting permission bits and owner fields when you see files you don't expect. This skill helps you validate backups, confirm file ownership, and find misplaced files. Listing Files with ls means use long, all, and human-readable options together to inspect file permissions, ownership, and sizes for effective troubleshooting.. In practical terms, use options to reveal hidden files, sizes, and ownership. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 2 › Chapter 1.3 › ls Options
Common options
Combine options for a richer listing.
ls
# Basic list of names

ls -l
# Long listing: permissions, owner, size, date

ls -a
# Show hidden files starting with a dot

ls -lh
# Long listing with human-readable sizes
Practice: run ls -alh in a directory with config files to see user dotfiles and file sizes at a glance.
Interpreting the output
  • Permission bits show read, write, and execute for user, group, and others.
  • Owner and group columns indicate who controls access.
  • Modification time helps identify recent changes.
Misconception: file size in bytes is hard to scan. Use human-readable option to interpret sizes quickly.

screens.title: Changing Directories with cd
screens.narratorSegment: Changing directories is core to efficient shell work. The change-directory command accepts absolute paths that begin at root, and relative paths which are resolved from your current location. Use dot to represent the current directory and double-dot to step up one level. The tilde is a shortcut to your home directory and the dash returns you to the previous directory. These shortcuts let you move quickly without typing long paths. For example, to reach /etc from anywhere, use an absolute path like change-directory slash etc; to move from /home/cohortiauser/projects to the scripts folder inside it, use a relative path like change-directory scripts. A common mistake is confusing relative and absolute paths, which can lead to running commands in the wrong location. Practice by navigating between two known directories, using change-directory dash to toggle, and confirm with print-working-directory. Over time these shortcuts save keystrokes and reduce errors when editing and testing files. Changing Directories with cd means use absolute paths for precision, relative paths for speed, and shortcuts (~ and -) to move quickly while confirming location with print-working-directory.. In practical terms, absolute paths, relative paths, special shortcuts, and practical tips. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 1.3 › cd Usage
Examples
cd /etc          # Absolute path to /etc
cd ../home        # Relative: up one, then into home
cd ~              # Go to your home directory
cd -              # Return to previous directory
cd .              # Stays in current directory
Practical tips
  • Use absolute paths when scripting to avoid ambiguity.
  • Use relative paths for quick navigation during interactive work.

screens.title: Copying and Moving Files: cp and mv

For directories, add the recursive option to copy so the entire subtree is duplicated. screens.title: Viewing File Content
screens.narratorSegment: Inspecting file content helps you understand system state and debug issues. The cat command prints an entire file to the terminal and is quick for small files. For larger files use a pager such as less which lets you scroll forward and backward and search; more is similar but usually only scrolls forward. A misconception is leaving a pager open and forgetting how to exit — remember that pressing q quits less or more. Use these viewers with care on binary or very large files to avoid terminal flooding. Practice combining viewers with list and path confirmation to inspect the right files safely. Quick commands

fullNarratorScript:
Welcome. In this lesson you will learn how Linux arranges files under a single root and how to use the basic commands that let you move around, examine, and manage files. Understanding the Filesystem Hierarchy Standard gives you a reliable mental map so you can predict where configuration files, binaries, logs, and user data live. You will practice confirming your current location, listing directory contents, changing directories with absolute and relative paths, and performing safe file operations like creating, copying, and moving items. We will also cover how to view file content and where to find help using manual pages and quick help flags. A strong grasp of these basics prevents common mistakes, like accidentally deleting important data. For example, the careful use of listing and confirming paths before running a removal command can save hours of recovery work. By the end, you'll be able to navigate confidently and follow a consistent workflow for routine maintenance and troubleshooting.

By the end of this chapter you'll be able to explain how the Linux Filesystem Hierarchy Standard organizes the system, and you'll use basic commands to move around and manage files. Specifically, you'll interpret directory roles such as where system binaries, configuration files, and user data live. You will use the print-working-directory command to confirm your location, the list command to inspect directory contents with useful options, and the change-directory command with absolute and relative paths. You'll also create, copy, move, and remove files and directories while applying safety checks to avoid data loss. Finally, you'll read manual pages and use quick help flags to discover command options independently. These skills are foundational: they let you perform routine administration, troubleshoot file locations, and learn new commands by exploring their documentation. Practically, that means you can navigate to a configuration file, examine it, make a backup copy, and restore it if needed — all without relying on a graphical interface.

This second objectives slide focuses on practice and safety. You'll run a hands-on sequence that creates a predictable directory structure, makes sample files, and uses listing and change-directory commands to verify locations. Practicing these steps builds muscle memory: first create directories, then create files inside them, and then try copying and renaming. When you delete items, you'll use safer alternatives to forceful deletion and learn to preview targets before removing them. You'll also learn common command-line shortcuts such as tilde for your home directory and dash to return to the previous directory. These shortcuts speed daily work and reduce typing errors. Finally, you will learn to consult manual pages and help flags to answer questions about command options instead of guessing. This habit turns every command into a self-contained learning opportunity and reduces risky experimentation on production systems.

The Filesystem Hierarchy Standard is the convention that gives every file and directory a predictable place on Linux systems. Rather than drive letters, Linux uses a single root, represented by a forward slash, and organizes everything below it. This consistency matters: if you need to edit system configuration on one distribution, your knowledge about where /etc or /var typically lives transfers to other distributions. For example, system-wide configuration files are kept in /etc while user home directories are under /home. Bin and sbin directories contain executable programs, with /bin holding essential user commands and /sbin containing administrative utilities. The habit of knowing where to look speeds troubleshooting and script writing. A common misconception is that distributions freely rearrange these directories — they do not; the FHS promotes compatibility. In practice, when you search for a log file, you’ll often check /var/log first. Knowing the FHS reduces guesswork and helps you write commands that are robust across systems. Reflect: when you need a configuration file, which top-level directories will you check first and why? Filesystem Hierarchy Standard (FHS) means a single root filesystem with standard top-level directories lets you predict where system and user files live across distributions.. In practical terms, what the fhs is and why a single root matters. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Linux separates the system-provided executables and libraries from user-installed programs and personal data. Directories like /bin and /sbin store essential binaries used during boot and repair; /lib and /lib64 contain shared libraries required by those programs. In contrast, /usr holds the wider set of utilities and applications, often in /usr/bin and /usr/local. Optional third-party packages sometimes live under /opt. Virtual, runtime, and kernel interfaces appear in /proc and /sys; these are not regular files but views into kernel and process state. A useful mental model is: if you need to run a system maintenance utility as an administrator, check /sbin or /usr/sbin; if you are looking for a user-level program, check /usr/bin or /usr/local/bin. A common error is editing files under /usr directly for package-installed software — prefer /usr/local or /opt for local additions. When you need to inspect libraries, look into /lib or /lib64. Understanding the distinction avoids collisions between packaged files and locally administered resources. System vs. User Directories means system executables and libraries live in protected directories; user utilities and optional software use /usr and /opt, keeping system files stable.. In practical terms, where executables, libraries, and virtual filesystems belong. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Beyond executables and libraries, several directories have distinct runtime or administrative roles. /etc stores system configuration files such as network or service settings; a careful edit here changes system behavior. /home holds personal user data — each account typically has its directory under /home. The root user's personal directory is /root. /var contains variable data like system logs and mail queues; monitor /var/log for troubleshooting. /tmp is for temporary files and usually gets cleared at reboot. Mount points such as /media and /mnt are used for removable devices or temporarily mounted filesystems. Virtual filesystems /proc and /sys present kernel and process information as readable files; for example, /proc exposes process IDs and kernel parameters. A frequent mistake is treating /proc or /sys as normal persistent storage — changes there affect kernel state or are ephemeral. When you need to mount a USB drive, look under /media or /mnt; when diagnosing services, check /etc for configs and /var/log for logs. Other Important Directories means /etc contains configs, /var contains logs, /tmp is ephemeral, and /proc and /sys expose kernel and process state as virtual filesystems.. In practical terms, /etc, /home, /var, /tmp, /media, /mnt, /proc, /sys. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

When you open a terminal you are placed in your home directory; this is your safe workspace. To confirm your exact location use the print-working-directory command which prints an absolute path from the root. Practically, this prevents running commands in the wrong place. For example, if print-working-directory outputs /home/cohortiauser, you know you are in your personal area and not in /etc or /var. The tilde symbol is a convenient shorthand for the home directory, so using change-directory tilde returns you to your home quickly. Another useful convenience is the dash argument which sends you back to the previous directory, useful when switching between two folders. A common mistake is assuming a graphical prompt aligns with the shell location; always confirm with print-working-directory. Below is a short code example you can type and try in a lab: watch how the path changes and use the dash shortcut to toggle. The habit of printing your working directory before destructive commands is a simple safety practice that pays off. Confirming Where You Are: pwd and Home Directory means use the print-working-directory command and the tilde and dash shortcuts to know and return to safe locations before running commands.. In practical terms, how to confirm your current working directory and use the home shortcut. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Listing the contents of a directory is one of the most frequent tasks. The list command in its basic form shows filenames, but combining options gives useful detail. For example, list with long format shows permissions, ownership, size, and modification time, which is essential when troubleshooting permission problems or identifying large files.
